page_checks.summary: Light give, make and do retain some ditransitive selection in light uses; light-verb versus noun PP attachment and lexical restrictions compared.
Light give has four recipient/indirect-object correspondences: sigh, kiss, advice, description; initial make frames introduced.
Light make selects noun-dependent PPs and sometimes an indirect object; make a donation is marginal in some double-object uses; have/take register and lexical inventories.
Light do combines with count and noncount nominals; verb argument-alternation taxonomy contrasts transitivity, ditransitivity and core/noncore functions.
Three two-dimensional alternation grids compare alignment and valency, plus separate versus combined complements; later sections exclude voice and subordinate clauses.
Conative at-PP alternates with direct object and often indicates attempted rather than successful contact; the difference is implicature-sensitive.
Directional complements may differ in endpoint/completeness, consultative/contest alternants differ pragmatically, and emitted substance and speech NPs alternate with PPs.
Emission alternation reverses source/theme roles across subject and object; Type III transitive/intransitive object omission taxonomy begins.
Instructional register permits unstated context objects; win allows contextual omitted contest but enjoy does not allow ordinary contextual event omission.
Lexically restricted omitted definite, reflexive and reciprocal objects with varied constraints; clothe and resemble exclude parallel omission.
Reciprocal omission need not entail symmetrical transitivity; body-part and human-object omission classes are distinguished from excluded verbs.
Specific-category and normal-category unexpressed objects; eat/drink/read normally allow intransitives while devour/peruse resist; activity and accomplishment readings differ.
Intransitive stems can license limited factitive/cognate objects and reactions; cognate noun modification and passive are construction-sensitive.
Type IV object-to-subject causative alternation for dynamic events, separate from related copular result states; destroy and die excluded in opposite directions.
Causative alternations vary by sense; positional stative and agentive movement patterns contrast with active-form semantic middles, not an English middle voice.
